title: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible subsets (the power set) using backtracking.
shortTitle: Subsets — include or exclude each element

s1_definition.profdef: The power set is generated by a depth-first backtracking that, at each index, records the current partial subset and then recurses on remaining elements. Each element is either taken or skipped, producing 2^n subsets. Adding the current path to the result at every node of the recursion tree (not only at leaves) yields all subsets including the empty set.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India offers n optional add-on services. A customer can pick any combination — none, some, or all. Listing every possible package is listing the power set: for each add-on you branch into "include it" and "leave it out," and every point along the way is a valid package.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each element choose include or exclude; record the path at every step to get all 2^n subsets.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The power set is generated by a depth-first backtracking that, at each index, records the current partial subset and then recurses on remaining elements. Each element is either taken or skipped, producing 2^n subsets. Adding the current path to the result at every node of the recursion tree (not only at leaves) yields all subsets including the empty set.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India offers n optional add-on services. A customer can pick any combination — none, some, or all. Listing every possible package is listing the power set: for each add-on you branch into "include it" and "leave it out," and every point along the way is a valid package.

**One line to remember:** For each element choose include or exclude; record the path at every step to get all 2^n subsets.

sections.s2_technical:
Use a recursive helper carrying a start index and the current path. At entry, record a copy of the path into the result; then loop from start to the end, add an element, recurse with the next index, and remove it (backtrack). For example: `result.add(new ArrayList<>(path)); for (int i=start;i<nums.length;i++){ path.add(nums[i]); backtrack(i+1); path.remove(path.size()-1); }`.

Recording at every entry (including the first, empty path) captures the empty subset and all sizes. Using `i+1` as the next start prevents reusing earlier elements and avoids permutations of the same subset.

The time is O(n · 2^n) because there are 2^n subsets and copying each costs up to n, and the recursion depth is n. A senior nuance is that an equivalent bitmask enumeration over 0..2^n-1 produces the same subsets iteratively, which some interviewers prefer for its lack of recursion.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a premium account bundles optional add-on services, and the product team wants to enumerate every possible add-on package to price them. This is exactly how generating subsets works.

Problem 2 — Every combination, including the empty package and the full package, is valid and must appear exactly once. This is exactly why the path is recorded at every recursion node and the start index advances.

The mini-project builds an `AddOnPackageGenerator`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three add-on ids: one, two, three.

Step 1: Entry records the empty package.

Step 2: Including one records [1], then including two records [1,2], then three records [1,2,3]; backtracking peels them off.

Step 3: After exhausting one's branch, the loop advances to start with two, recording [2] and [2,3], then with three recording [3].

Step 4: The eight packages are the full power set, generated once each.

2026-10-26T23:45:00Z [INFO] Package: [1]
2026-10-26T23:45:00Z [INFO] Package: [1, 2]
2026-10-26T23:45:00Z [INFO] Package: [1, 2, 3]

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  backtrack(start=0, path=[])
    record []            ─┐
    +1 → record [1] → +2 [1,2] → +3 [1,2,3]  (deepest)
             backtrack     ...
    +2 → [2] → [2,3]
    +3 → [3]
  total = 2^3 = 8 subsets
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Subsets, or the power set, is the foundational backtracking problem. I use a recursive helper that carries a start index and the current partial subset, and the single most important detail is that I record a copy of the path at every node of the recursion, not only at the leaves, which is what captures the empty set and every intermediate size. Inside the loop I take an element, recurse with the next index, and then remove it to backtrack, exploring the include-and-exclude choice for each element.

Advancing the start index by one on each recursive call is what prevents reusing earlier elements and stops me from generating permutations of the same subset. The whole thing is O(n times 2 to the n), because there are 2 to the n subsets and copying each costs up to n.

In my project at National Bank of India, the product team needed to enumerate every possible package of optional account add-ons in order to price each combination, and this backtracking generated the complete catalog of packages exactly once each. When an interviewer prefers an iterative approach, I mention that a bitmask enumeration over zero to 2-to-the-n-minus-one produces the identical set without recursion.
